text: This chapter has built toward a real tension. Data gravity pulls compute toward wherever data already lives. Sovereignty requirements can legally pin data to specific regions. And yet enterprises genuinely want one single data platform -- one consistent way to query and govern their data no matter which cloud someone's working in. This lesson resolves that tension.

The resolution is that a single platform doesn't require a single physical copy. It means one consistent format and one consistent catalog -- not one storage location. You can have one logical platform while the actual bytes stay wherever gravity or sovereignty require.

That's what a lakehouse architecture does. Data sits as files in cloud object storage -- Azure Data Lake Storage or S3 -- using an open table format like Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, or Apache Hudi, which adds schema, transactions, and time travel on top of plain files. The payoff: any compute engine that understands the format -- Databricks Spark, Snowflake, Trino, Athena, Microsoft Fabric -- can read the same tables, regardless of which cloud that engine runs in. Storage and compute are no longer the same product.

But open files alone aren't enough -- something has to track which tables exist, their schema, and who can touch them, consistently across clouds. That's the catalog's job. Databricks Unity Catalog spans workspaces across AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud with one governance model. The Iceberg REST catalog is an open standard letting Snowflake, Databricks, and Trino all read the same tables through one interface. Snowflake's own cross-cloud replication keeps data synchronized across providers, presented as one account. The catalog, not the storage bucket, is what makes the platform feel singular.

None of this erases gravity or sovereignty. Real deployments still partition data deliberately by region or domain, replicate only small reference tables at the table level where needed, and let one catalog present a unified namespace over data that's physically scattered exactly where cost and compliance require it to be.

Get this backward -- chase one global physical copy of everything -- and you'll fight egress cost, latency, and sovereignty law all at once for no real benefit. Get it right, and an analyst queries one consistent platform while the data underneath quietly respects where it actually needs to live. Next chapter turns to the other side of running across multiple clouds: getting one unified view of cost and governance across Azure, AWS, and on-prem.
